strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated application (visual prostheses for blind individuals) with clear societal impact
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG) with both within-subject and cross-subject protocols
Solid ablation studies (Tables 5-8) demonstrating the contribution of cross-attention mechanisms over simpler alternatives (FCC: 0.188 vs 0.213)
Extensive visualization analysis with detailed topography comparisons that provide good intuition about spatial patterns and subject-specific variations
Clear and well-structured presentation of methodology with detailed technical descriptions in Section 3
Multimodal capability handling both EEG and MEG signals demonstrates framework versatility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty for a top-tier ML venue - primarily combines existing components (pre-trained CLIP encoder, standard U-Net diffusion model, known cross-attention mechanisms) without introducing fundamentally new methods

Modest performance metrics with high absolute error: within-subject MSE of 0.217 (suggesting ~22% error) and FCC of 0.188 indicate weak correlation with actual signals; unclear if such error levels would preserve visual information for functional restoration

Severe cross-subject generalization failure: FCC drops dramatically from within-subject (0.192-0.231) to cross-subject (0.018-0.095) with substantial inter-subject variability; no solutions proposed despite this being critical for clinical prosthesis application

Biological plausibility claimed but insufficiently validated - only topography visualization comparisons provided; no comparison to known neuroscience principles of visual processing; no evidence reconstructed signals would elicit intended visual perception
Missing direct quantitative comparison to Lu & Golomb (2024), acknowledged as most similar prior work; only dimensional differences noted without performance comparison
Limited dataset scale (10 EEG subjects, 4 MEG subjects, 1,654 training concepts) and incomplete ablations on key architectural choices (cross-attention dimension, placement, layer configuration)

Reproducibility concerns including lack of code availability statement, incomplete preprocessing details beyond reference to Song et al. (2025), and unspecified dataset availability for other researchers

No validation that reconstructed signals would support actual visual perception - missing perceptual evaluation, user studies, or analysis of functional signal quality metrics required for prosthesis application
Dense and difficult-to-interpret visualizations (Figures 5-8) that require extensive caption reading for insight extraction
Absence of statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or formal variance decomposition analysis despite reporting standard deviations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in visual prosthetics where brain encoding lags behind brain decoding; uses real M/EEG signals as supervision rather than just images

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two datasets with multiple appropriate metrics (MSE, Pearson, Cosine, Synchronization Likelihood), both within-subject and cross-subject protocols, plus thorough ablation studies
Clear and well-justified methodology combining cross-attention mechanisms, CLIP+text unified embeddings, and spatio-temporal position embeddings with neuroscience motivation
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, preprocessing steps, and algorithms in appendices
Generally clear presentation with effective figures (especially architecture diagram) and comprehensive supplementary material
weaknesses: Severe cross-subject generalization failure (Pearson correlation drops from 0.425 to 0.157 for EEG, 0.379 to 0.082 for MEG)—an ~80% performance loss that critically undermines practical applicability for visual prosthetics where per-subject training may be infeasible; paper acknowledges but offers no solutions

Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (DiT, DDIM, CLIP, cross-attention, LLMs) without fundamental methodological innovation; contribution is architectural engineering rather than new insights

LLM-generated caption injection poorly justified: unclear why LLM captions are necessary when CLIP already captures semantics; no comparison to alternative text sources (dataset captions, labels); adds computational overhead and error potential without clear evidence of necessity

Brain region partitioning appears ad-hoc: five regions defined for both EEG/MEG without justification; severe channel imbalance (EEG occipital: 3 channels vs. frontal: 22); no comparison of alternative partitioning schemes; unclear how generalizes across anatomical variability

Claims of 'biological plausibility' unsupported: evaluation measures signal similarity to ground truth (MSE, Pearson, Cosine), not actual biological validity; missing frequency domain analysis (power spectral density, oscillations), inter-channel patterns, temporal dynamics, and validation that generated signals produce appropriate visual percepts

Limited baseline comparisons: only three baselines (two from 2014-2015, one adapted from fMRI); no comparisons to other neural encoding models, diffusion variants, VAE/flow-based approaches, or subject-specific transfer learning
Statistical significance not reported: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; cannot determine if improvements over baselines are statistically meaningful

Gap between motivation and practical applicability: introduces visual prosthetics application but leaves critical questions unaddressed: real-time computational costs, device calibration with poor cross-subject performance, sensitivity to preprocessing and electrode placement variability

Design choices under-explored: deterministic DDIM sampling chosen without ablation; concatenation for image-text fusion not compared to alternatives; no sensitivity analysis for patch size on vastly different scales (EEG 1008 patches vs MEG 3400 patches)

Potential train-test contamination: unclear whether test images from THINGS-EEG2 represent unseen concepts or just different samples of training concepts, affecting generalization interpretation; missing mechanistic analysis of what representations learned, whether they align with visual hierarchy, failure modes

strengths: Technically sound implementation of diffusion models with appropriate architectural choices (DiT, cross-attention, spatio-temporal embeddings)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, LLM comparisons, and brain region analysis
Well-structured presentation with clear figures and detailed reproducibility information in appendices
Demonstrates consistent within-subject performance improvements over reasonable baselines on two datasets
weaknesses: Misleading framing about visual prostheses application: generating M/EEG responses differs fundamentally from generating electrode stimulation patterns needed for prosthetics; connection to actual prosthetic function is never established
Severe cross-subject generalization failure (63-78% performance drop) makes method impractical for real-world use; paper identifies but does not solve this critical issue
Claims of 'biologically plausible' signal generation lack adequate validation; evaluation metrics measure similarity to ground truth, not biological validity or ability to evoke appropriate percepts
Limited methodological novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (DiT, CLIP, cross-attention, LLMs) without significant algorithmic or architectural innovation
Narrow experimental scope: only two related datasets from THINGS project; no cross-dataset validation or generalization studies to different stimulus types
Redundant use of both CLIP image embeddings and LLM text embeddings with only modest ablation improvements (~1-2%), raising questions about necessity and design choices
Insufficient baseline comparisons: primarily compared to SynBrain (designed for fMRI, questionable adaptation) and 2014-2015 methods; missing comparisons to recent diffusion-based approaches
No mechanistic insights into what the model learns about visual encoding or why it fails at cross-subject generalization; limited analysis beyond reporting metrics

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem (brain encoding for visual prostheses) with practical medical significance
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including within-subject and cross-subject settings, multiple complementary metrics (MSE, Pearson, Cosine, SL), and thorough ablation studies
Strong within-subject results with substantial improvements over baselines across all evaluation metrics (e.g., Pearson 0.425 vs 0.366 for SynBrain)

Well-motivated technical design: spatio-temporal position embeddings explicitly model hierarchical visual processing and temporal dynamics; unified visual-semantic embeddings appropriately combine visual and semantic information
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices documenting preprocessing, training algorithms, hyperparameters, and dataset details enabling reproduction
Clear presentation and honest discussion of limitations, including transparent reporting of cross-subject performance degradation
Solid ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component with brain region analysis confirming neuroscientific expectations
weaknesses: Severe cross-subject generalization failure: Pearson correlation drops 63% for EEG (0.425→0.157) and 78% for MEG (0.379→0.082), critically limiting practical prosthesis deployment which requires personalization; paper offers no concrete solutions beyond mentioning future research
Limited methodological novelty: combines established techniques (DiT, cross-attention, CLIP, LLMs) with primary contribution being application rather than fundamental innovation

Biological plausibility claims unsupported: evaluation uses statistical similarity metrics rather than validating whether generated signals evoke appropriate visual percepts through prosthetic stimulation; cross-subject results suggest lack of necessary personalized biological properties

Limited dataset diversity: only two THINGS-based datasets with simple object stimuli, small sample sizes (10 EEG subjects, 4 MEG participants), no evaluation on complex natural scenes or patient data with actual visual impairment

Missing critical analyses: no inference time/computational cost discussion (important for real-time prosthesis), limited failure case analysis, no comparison with simpler baselines (non-diffusion generative models, direct regression)

Heavy LLM caption dependency with no robustness analysis: no investigation of performance with poor captions or images LLMs fail to describe; potential distribution mismatch between precomputed training captions and test data unexplored

Incomplete evaluation: statistical metrics (MSE, Cosine) lack clear connection to visual perception quality; correlation and SL measure signal similarity but not functional correctness for prosthesis control; no perceptual validation or psychophysical testing
Suboptimal baseline comparisons: SynBrain designed for fMRI not M/EEG so adaptation may be suboptimal; missing recent diffusion-based decoding methods and simpler generative model baselines
